title: Maine Civics & Government (8th Grade)
description: Maine Civics & Government (8th Grade) practice - 100 questions. 70 federal civics questions plus a 30-question Maine layer: Maine Constitution and government, town meeting and municipal government, the citizen initiative, People's Veto and ranked-choice voting, and a Wabanaki studies block (Penobscot Nation, Passamaquoddy Tribe, Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, Mi'kmaq Nation, the Wabanaki Confederacy, treaty history, the Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act of 1980, and contemporary tribal sovereignty) per 20-A M.R.S. sec. 4706.

questions.question: A student asks why no state law, city rule, or even act of Congress can override the nation's founding charter. That charter, the supreme law of the land, is:
questions.correctAnswer: The U.S. Constitution
questions.explanation: The Constitution, written in 1787 and ratified in 1788, sits above every other law in the United States. When a law conflicts with it, courts can strike that law down.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Constitution outranks every other law.

img.scene: A large parchment document resting under glass in a museum case, lit warmly from above. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The Constitution outranks every other law.
img.title: THE SUPREME LAW

questions.question: Before the Constitution, the young United States was governed by a loose confederation whose central government could not tax or enforce its decisions. That first framework was called:
questions.correctAnswer: The Articles of Confederation
questions.explanation: The Articles of Confederation (ratified 1781) created a weak central government - Congress could ask states for money but not compel payment - which is why leaders met in Philadelphia in 1787 to design a stronger system.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Articles were too loose to hold.

img.scene: Thirteen separate wooden chairs arranged in a loose wide circle in an empty colonial meeting hall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The Articles were too loose to hold.
img.title: THE FIRST FRAMEWORK

questions.question: In 1787, delegates from twelve states gathered in Philadelphia for a meeting that produced the Constitution. That meeting is known as:
questions.correctAnswer: The Constitutional Convention
questions.explanation: The Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787. Delegates who had been sent to revise the Articles instead drafted an entirely new Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Philadelphia, 1787: a new plan is drafted.

img.scene: A long wooden table in a bright colonial assembly room with quills, ink pots and empty chairs along both sides. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Philadelphia, 1787: a new plan is drafted.
img.title: PHILADELPHIA, 1787

questions.question: A civics teacher writes three goals on the board - form a more perfect union, establish justice, ensure domestic tranquility. These phrases come from the part of the Constitution called:
questions.correctAnswer: The Preamble
questions.explanation: The Preamble is the Constitution's one-paragraph introduction. It states the purposes of the government the document creates, beginning 'We the People of the United States.'
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Preamble states the purposes first.

img.scene: An open book on a lectern in a quiet library, its first page blank, morning light across the desk. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The Preamble states the purposes first.
img.title: WE THE PEOPLE

questions.question: Why does the Constitution divide power among three separate branches instead of giving it all to one leader?
questions.correctAnswer: So each branch can check the others and no single person or group can control the whole government
distractors: So laws can be passed more quickly
So the president can delegate unpopular decisions
So states do not need their own governments
questions.explanation: Separation of powers, drawn from Montesquieu, assigns lawmaking to Congress, enforcement to the executive, and judging to the courts. Each branch holds tools to limit the others, which protects liberty.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three branches, each watching the others.

img.scene: A balance scale with three equal stone pillars standing behind it against a plain sky. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Three branches, each watching the others.
img.title: POWER, DIVIDED ON PURPOSE

questions.question: Late in a session, the president returns a transportation bill unsigned, with written objections. The House then votes by well over two-thirds to enact it anyway, and the Senate follows with its own two-thirds vote. Congress has just exercised:
questions.correctAnswer: A check the legislative branch holds over the executive branch
questions.explanation: The veto override is one of the Constitution's checks and balances: Congress can enact a law over the president's objection with a two-thirds vote in the House and the Senate.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds can override a veto.

img.scene: A heavy wooden veto stamp resting beside a tall stack of paper ballots in a legislative chamber. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds can override a veto.
img.title: THE VETO OVERRIDE

questions.question: When the Supreme Court declared a law unconstitutional in Marbury v. Madison (1803), it established the power known as:
questions.correctAnswer: Judicial review
questions.explanation: In Marbury v. Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall's Court claimed the power to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution - judicial review, the judiciary's central check on the other branches.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Marbury gave courts the review power.

img.scene: A marble courthouse facade with tall columns seen from the bottom of wide stone steps. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Marbury gave courts the review power.
img.title: MARBURY V. MADISON

questions.question: A governor and a president both claim authority over the same policy area, and the Constitution gives that power to neither level exclusively. Powers shared this way are called:
questions.correctAnswer: Concurrent powers
questions.explanation: Federalism divides power between the national and state governments. Concurrent powers - like taxing, building roads, and running courts - are exercised by both levels at once.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Shared powers are concurrent powers.

img.scene: Two overlapping circles of light cast on a wooden floor by two lamps. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Shared powers are concurrent powers.
img.title: SHARED POWER

questions.question: The Tenth Amendment protects state authority by declaring that powers not given to the federal government and not denied to the states are:
questions.correctAnswer: Reserved to the states or to the people
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment, part of the Bill of Rights, reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people - the constitutional basis for state control of areas like education and local policing.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: What is not delegated is reserved.

img.scene: A row of many different state-shaped wooden blocks lined up on a shelf, each a different color. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: What is not delegated is reserved.
img.title: THE TENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: If a state law directly conflicts with a valid federal law on the same subject, which one wins under the Constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: The federal law, under the Supremacy Clause of Article VI
distractors: The state law, under the Tenth Amendment
questions.explanation: Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties 'the supreme Law of the Land.' State judges must follow federal law when the two genuinely conflict.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Article VI settles conflicts for federal law.

img.scene: Two stacks of law books on a scale, the taller bound volume resting higher than the smaller one. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Article VI settles conflicts for federal law.
img.title: THE SUPREMACY CLAUSE

questions.question: When the first Congress proposed a dozen amendments in 1789, the states ratified ten of them by December 1791 - safeguarding speech, arms, juries, due process and more. That ratified set of ten is known together as:
questions.correctAnswer: The Bill of Rights
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists demanded protections for individual rights as the price of ratification. James Madison guided ten amendments through Congress, and the states ratified them in 1791.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ten amendments guard individual liberty.

img.scene: Ten framed parchment panels hanging in a row on a museum wall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Ten amendments guard individual liberty.
img.title: THE BILL OF RIGHTS

questions.question: A newspaper prints an editorial harshly criticizing a mayor, and the mayor orders the paper shut down. Which amendment most directly forbids that?
questions.correctAnswer: The First Amendment
questions.explanation: The First Amendment protects freedom of the press, along with speech, religion, assembly, and petition. Government may not silence a publication for criticizing officials.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The First protects the critical press.

img.scene: A vintage printing press in a workshop with blank sheets of paper stacked beside it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The First protects the critical press.
img.title: FREEDOM OF THE PRESS

questions.question: Detectives believe stolen property sits inside a suspect's apartment, but no judge has signed any paper authorizing them to enter. Under the Fourth Amendment, investigators must generally first obtain:
questions.correctAnswer: A warrant based on probable cause, describing the place to be searched
distractors: A two-thirds vote of the city council
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment bars unreasonable searches and seizures. A warrant must rest on probable cause and particularly describe the place to be searched and the things to be seized.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No warrant, no general search.

img.scene: A magnifying glass resting on a plain wooden desk beside a sealed envelope. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: No warrant, no general search.
img.title: THE FOURTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A defendant refuses to answer questions in court, saying, 'I plead the Fifth.' The Fifth Amendment protects against:
questions.correctAnswer: Being forced to testify against yourself - self-incrimination
distractors: Being charged with a crime at all
questions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment guarantees that no person 'shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself.' It also guarantees due process and grand-jury indictment for serious federal crimes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fifth lets you stay silent.

img.scene: An empty witness chair in a wood-paneled courtroom, a single lamp glowing above it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The Fifth lets you stay silent.
img.title: PLEADING THE FIFTH

questions.question: Clarence Gideon, too poor to hire counsel, was forced to defend himself at his Florida felony trial, then appealed with a handwritten petition. The Supreme Court's 1963 ruling in his case requires states to provide a poor defendant:
questions.correctAnswer: A lawyer, free of charge, under the Sixth Amendment
questions.explanation: Clarence Gideon's handwritten appeal led the Court to hold that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies to the states, so an indigent defendant must be given an attorney.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Gideon: counsel even if you cannot pay.

img.scene: A single handwritten letter in pencil resting on a courtroom table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Gideon: counsel even if you cannot pay.
img.title: GIDEON V. WAINWRIGHT

questions.question: The Sixth Amendment's promise of a 'speedy and public trial' also includes the right to:
questions.correctAnswer: An impartial jury and to be informed of the charges against you
questions.explanation: The Sixth Amendment guarantees a speedy, public trial by an impartial jury, notice of the accusation, the chance to confront witnesses, and the assistance of counsel.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Speedy, public, impartial: the Sixth.

img.scene: Rows of empty wooden jury-box chairs in a bright courtroom. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Speedy, public, impartial: the Sixth.
img.title: THE SIXTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A judge sets bail at ten million dollars for a minor shoplifting charge. The Eighth Amendment is relevant because it forbids:
questions.correctAnswer: Excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments
distractors: Any fine over one hundred dollars
Prison sentences longer than a year
questions.explanation: The Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments. Bail wildly out of proportion to a minor charge is the classic example.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Eighth limits bail and punishment.

img.scene: A small set of iron keys hanging on a hook beside a plain stone wall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The Eighth limits bail and punishment.
img.title: THE EIGHTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, transformed the Bill of Rights by:
questions.correctAnswer: Requiring states, not just the federal government, to respect due process and equal protection
questions.explanation: The Fourteenth Amendment defines citizenship and forbids states to deny due process or equal protection of the laws. Through it, most Bill of Rights protections have been applied against state governments.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fourteenth binds the states too.

img.scene: A stone archway with light passing through it onto a path on the far side. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The Fourteenth binds the states too.
img.title: THE FOURTEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: At the close of the Civil War, an amendment permanently ended slavery and involuntary servitude in every state of the restored Union, North and South alike. Ratified in December 1865, that amendment is:
questions.correctAnswer: The Thirteenth Amendment (1865)
questions.explanation: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865, abolished slavery and involuntary servitude everywhere in the United States, except as punishment for a crime.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Thirteen ended slavery.

img.scene: A heavy iron chain with one link broken open, lying on a wooden surface. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Thirteen ended slavery.
img.title: THE THIRTEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: An amendment added in 1870 specifically prohibits states from using race, color, or previous condition of servitude to keep citizens away from the ballot box. That amendment is:
questions.correctAnswer: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870)
questions.explanation: The Fifteenth Amendment bars denying or abridging the right to vote 'on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.' Later laws, like the Voting Rights Act of 1965, were needed to enforce it fully.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fifteen: no racial voting bars.

img.scene: A row of plain paper ballots being slipped into a wooden ballot box. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Fifteen: no racial voting bars.
img.title: THE FIFTEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: For most of American history, United States senators were chosen by state legislatures. Direct election of senators by the voters was established by:
questions.correctAnswer: The Seventeenth Amendment (1913)
questions.explanation: The Seventeenth Amendment moved Senate elections from state legislatures to the people, one of the major democratic reforms of the Progressive Era.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Seventeen put senators on the ballot.

img.scene: Citizens standing in line at a polling place in a school gymnasium, seen from behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Seventeen put senators on the ballot.
img.title: DIRECT ELECTION OF SENATORS

questions.question: Suffragists picketed outside the White House and marched for decades. Their campaign succeeded when a 1920 amendment finally prohibited denying any citizen the ballot on account of sex. That amendment is:
questions.correctAnswer: The Nineteenth Amendment (1920)
questions.explanation: The Nineteenth Amendment forbids denying the vote on account of sex. It was the product of a seventy-year suffrage movement and was ratified in August 1920.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nineteen: women's suffrage.

img.scene: A white sash and a bouquet of yellow roses resting on a wooden chair. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Nineteen: women's suffrage.
img.title: THE NINETEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: During the Vietnam War, eighteen-year-olds could be drafted but in many states could not vote. The amendment that set the national voting age at eighteen is:
questions.correctAnswer: The Twenty-Sixth Amendment (1971)
questions.explanation: The Twenty-Sixth Amendment, the fastest ever ratified, lowered the voting age to eighteen in 1971 under the slogan 'old enough to fight, old enough to vote.'
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Twenty-Six set voting at eighteen.

img.scene: A young first-time voter receiving a small round sticker from an election worker's hand. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Twenty-Six set voting at eighteen.
img.title: VOTING AT EIGHTEEN

questions.question: Changing the Constitution requires an amendment. Under Article V, an amendment must be proposed by two-thirds of Congress (or a convention) and then:
questions.correctAnswer: Ratified by three-fourths of the states
distractors: Ratified by a simple majority of states
questions.explanation: Article V's two-step process - proposal and ratification by three-fourths of the states - has produced only twenty-seven amendments in more than two centuries.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds propose, three-fourths ratify.

img.scene: Many state flags hanging in a long hall, viewed from one end so they recede into the distance uncountably. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds propose, three-fourths ratify.
img.title: AMENDING THE CONSTITUTION

questions.question: A bill becomes a law at the federal level only after it has been:
questions.correctAnswer: Passed by both houses of Congress in identical form and signed by the president, or passed over a veto
distractors: Published in newspapers for thirty days
questions.explanation: Both the House and the Senate must pass the same text. The president may sign it or veto it; Congress may override a veto with two-thirds of both houses.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Same text, both houses, then the president.

img.scene: Two long rows of empty desks facing each other in a legislative chamber. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Same text, both houses, then the president.
img.title: HOW A BILL BECOMES LAW

questions.question: Congress is bicameral - it has two chambers. They are:
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives and the Senate
distractors: The House of Commons and the House of Lords
questions.explanation: The Great Compromise of 1787 created a House based on population and a Senate with equal state representation. Together they form the legislative branch.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two chambers: House and Senate.

img.scene: A grand building with a domed center and two long wings extending on either side. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Two chambers: House and Senate.
img.title: A TWO-CHAMBER CONGRESS

questions.question: Representation in the House of Representatives is based on each state's population, adjusted after every census. A state's number of House seats therefore:
questions.correctAnswer: Can grow or shrink every ten years as its population changes relative to other states
distractors: Is always equal to its number of counties
questions.explanation: The census every ten years drives reapportionment: states gaining population gain House seats and Electoral College votes; states losing population can lose them. Maine currently has two House seats.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The census moves House seats.

img.scene: A census worker's clipboard and pencil resting on a porch railing. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The census moves House seats.
img.title: THE CENSUS AND SEATS

questions.question: Tiny Rhode Island and enormous California receive exactly the same representation in one chamber of Congress, regardless of how many people live in each. In that chamber, how many seats does the Constitution allot to each state?
questions.correctAnswer: Two senators
distractors: A number set by its governor
questions.explanation: Equal Senate representation was the small states' condition in the Great Compromise. Every state has two senators, each serving a six-year term.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Every state: two senators.

img.scene: Two tall marble columns standing side by side in front of a courthouse. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Every state: two senators.
img.title: TWO SENATORS EACH

questions.question: A newly elected member of the House of Representatives will face the voters again in just:
questions.correctAnswer: Two years - House terms are two years long
questions.explanation: The House's two-year term keeps representatives close to the people. The entire House is elected every two years, including in midterm elections.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House members run every two years.

img.scene: A calendar page and a campaign yard sign leaning against a fence. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: House members run every two years.
img.title: THE TWO-YEAR HOUSE TERM

questions.question: Treaties negotiated by the president do not take effect until they receive:
questions.correctAnswer: The approval of two-thirds of the Senate
questions.explanation: The Senate's advice-and-consent power covers treaties (two-thirds required) and confirmation of presidential appointments such as cabinet secretaries and federal judges.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate.

img.scene: Two diplomats' chairs facing each other across a small polished table with a flag on it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate.
img.title: ADVICE AND CONSENT

questions.question: Only one chamber of Congress may begin a trial to remove a president - and only after the other chamber has impeached. Removal trials are held by:
questions.correctAnswer: The Senate, with conviction requiring two-thirds of senators
questions.explanation: The House impeaches by majority vote; the Senate tries the case, and two-thirds of senators must vote to convict and remove. No president has ever been removed this way.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The House charges, the Senate tries.

img.scene: A gavel resting on a sounding block on a polished wooden desk. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The House charges, the Senate tries.
img.title: IMPEACHMENT AND TRIAL

questions.question: The branch of government that commands the armed forces, enforces federal laws, and conducts foreign policy is:
questions.correctAnswer: The executive branch, headed by the president
questions.explanation: Article II vests executive power in the president, who serves as commander in chief, chief diplomat, and the official responsible for taking care that the laws are faithfully executed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The president leads the executive branch.

img.scene: Exactly three stone pillars of equal height standing in a row on a plaza. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The president leads the executive branch.
img.title: THREE BRANCHES

questions.question: If a president dies, resigns, or is removed, the Constitution provides that the office passes to:
questions.correctAnswer: The vice president
questions.explanation: The Twenty-Fifth Amendment confirms that the vice president becomes president, not merely acting president. The Presidential Succession Act places the Speaker and others further down the line.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The vice president steps up first.

img.scene: An empty presidential desk chair in an oval office, seen from the side. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The vice president steps up first.
img.title: PRESIDENTIAL SUCCESSION

questions.question: A president is elected not by the national popular vote directly but by the Electoral College. The number of electors a state has equals:
questions.correctAnswer: Its total number of members of Congress - House seats plus its two senators
distractors: Its land area in square miles
questions.explanation: Each state's electors equal its congressional delegation. With the District of Columbia's three, there are 538 electors, and 270 electoral votes win the presidency. Maine awards two electors by congressional district and two statewide.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Electors equal the delegation size.

img.scene: A large map board with pins clustered in different regions, too many pins to count. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Electors equal the delegation size.
img.title: THE ELECTORAL COLLEGE

questions.question: The heads of the executive departments - State, Treasury, Defense, and others - who advise the president are known collectively as:
questions.correctAnswer: The Cabinet
questions.explanation: Cabinet secretaries are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate. The Cabinet grew from four officers in Washington's administration to fifteen department heads today.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Cabinet advises the president.

img.scene: A long conference table with many empty high-backed chairs in a formal room. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The Cabinet advises the president.
img.title: THE PRESIDENT'S CABINET

questions.question: Without asking Congress to vote on anything, a president signs a directive ordering every federal agency to change the way it purchases its vehicle fleet. Because the directive comes from the president alone and binds the executive branch, it counts as:
questions.correctAnswer: Issued by the president alone to direct the executive branch, without a vote of Congress
distractors: Passed by both houses of Congress
questions.explanation: Executive orders carry the force of law inside the executive branch, but they rest on the president's constitutional or statutory authority, can be reversed by a later president, and can be struck down by courts.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Orders direct; Congress legislates.

img.scene: A fountain pen resting on a single sheet of paper on a wide desk. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Orders direct; Congress legislates.
img.title: EXECUTIVE ORDERS

questions.question: The judicial branch decides cases under the Constitution and federal law. Its highest court is:
questions.correctAnswer: The Supreme Court of the United States
distractors: The Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court is the only court the Constitution itself creates. Congress established the lower federal courts - district courts and courts of appeals - beneath it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One court sits at the top.

img.scene: Nine high-backed chairs in a row behind a long mahogany bench in a marble courtroom. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: One court sits at the top.
img.title: THE SUPREME COURT

questions.question: Federal judges hold their offices for life, subject to good behavior. The Framers chose life tenure mainly so that judges could:
questions.correctAnswer: Decide cases without fear of political pressure or losing their jobs for unpopular rulings
questions.explanation: Life tenure and protected salaries insulate judges from the political branches, supporting an independent judiciary - balanced by impeachment as a removal tool for misconduct.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Life tenure protects independent judging.

img.scene: A judge's robe hanging on a wooden stand in a quiet chamber. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Life tenure protects independent judging.
img.title: AN INDEPENDENT JUDICIARY

questions.question: A person charged with a serious federal crime has the right to have the accusation screened by a grand jury, and at trial to be judged by:
questions.correctAnswer: A trial jury of ordinary citizens, whose guilty verdict in federal court must be unanimous
distractors: A panel of three judges only
A military tribunal in all cases
questions.explanation: The jury system puts citizens between the government and the accused. Federal criminal verdicts must be unanimous, and the Sixth Amendment guarantees the jury will be impartial.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Citizens judge the accused's guilt.

img.scene: Empty wooden jury chairs in two rows inside a courtroom. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Citizens judge the accused's guilt.
img.title: JUDGED BY A JURY

questions.question: Citizenship in the United States can be acquired by birth in the country or through the legal process called:
questions.correctAnswer: Naturalization
questions.explanation: The Fourteenth Amendment makes anyone born or naturalized in the United States a citizen. Naturalization requires lawful residence, good character, knowledge of English and U.S. civics, and an oath of allegiance.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Naturalization makes new citizens.

img.scene: A group of new citizens holding small flags at an outdoor ceremony, seen from behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Naturalization makes new citizens.
img.title: BECOMING A CITIZEN

questions.question: Everyone living in the country, citizen or not, must obey its laws and pay its taxes. Which pair of civic duties, by contrast, is reserved solely to citizens?
questions.correctAnswer: Serving on a jury when called (and voting in federal elections)
questions.explanation: Jurors are drawn from the citizenry, and federal ballots may be cast only by citizens. Law-abidingness and taxpaying, by contrast, are demanded of every resident, whatever their status.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Juries and the ballot: citizens' duties.

img.scene: A jury summons envelope and a voter registration card side by side on a table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Juries and the ballot: citizens' duties.
img.title: DUTIES OF CITIZENS

questions.question: In the American system, 'the rule of law' means that:
questions.correctAnswer: Everyone - including government officials - must obey the law, and no one is above it
distractors: The president may ignore court rulings
Laws apply only to ordinary citizens
questions.explanation: The rule of law is the principle that government is bound by its own rules: officials must follow the law and the Constitution just as private citizens must.

questions.correctAnswer: Ranks candidates in order of preference, and ballots for eliminated candidates transfer to the voter's next choice until someone holds a majority
distractors: Must vote for only one party's candidates
Votes twice in two separate elections
Lets a computer choose randomly among finalists
questions.explanation: Maine voters approved ranked-choice voting by initiative in 2016. It is used in primaries and in general elections for federal offices - after state court rulings, it does not apply to the general election for governor or state legislature.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rank them; ballots transfer to a majority.

img.tip: T-Rexy says: Rank them; ballots transfer to a majority.

questions.question: Why did Maine voters adopt these direct-democracy tools - initiative, People's Veto, and later ranked-choice voting?
questions.correctAnswer: Reformers believed the Legislature alone could not be trusted to act on popular measures, so the constitution gives final lawmaking power on referred questions to the voters
distractors: The federal government required Maine to adopt them
Maine's constitution forbids legislatures from passing laws
They were copied from the Articles of Confederation
questions.explanation: The 1908 amendments were a Progressive Era reform, driven by frustration with a Legislature seen as captive to corporate interests. Maine remains one of about half the states with a statewide initiative process.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Reform put final say with voters.

img.tip: T-Rexy says: Reform put final say with voters.
img.title: POWER TO THE VOTERS

questions.question: The Wabanaki - 'People of the Dawnland' - are a confederacy of Native nations of the Northeast. The four federally recognized tribal nations located in Maine today are:
questions.correctAnswer: The Penobscot Nation, the Passamaquoddy Tribe, the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, and the Mi'kmaq Nation
distractors: The Penobscot Nation, the Cherokee Nation, the Navajo Nation, and the Sioux
The Passamaquoddy Tribe, the Iroquois Confederacy, the Seminole Tribe, and the Apache
The Penobscot Nation, the Wampanoag Tribe, the Narragansett Tribe, and the Pequot
questions.explanation: These four nations - Penobscot, Passamaquoddy, Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, and Mi'kmaq Nation - are the federally recognized tribes in Maine. Their homelands span the Penobscot River, Passamaquoddy Bay, the St. John valley, and Aroostook County, and their citizens hold tribal, state, and United States citizenship together.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Four nations are recognized in Maine.

img.tip: T-Rexy says: Four nations are recognized in Maine.
img.title: FOUR NATIONS IN MAINE

questions.question: The name 'Wabanaki' means 'People of the Dawnland.' The name reflects the fact that the Wabanaki nations live:
questions.correctAnswer: In the far Northeast, among the first lands in the region to see the dawn sun
questions.explanation: Wabanaki homelands - Wabanakiak - cover what is now Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, and Canada's Maritime provinces. Their eastern position means the dawn reaches them first.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Dawnland: first light in the East.

questions.question: The Penobscot Nation's homeland centers on the Penobscot River. Its seat of government is located at:
questions.correctAnswer: Indian Island, in the Penobscot River near Old Town
distractors: The city of Bangor's city hall
A reservation in New Brunswick only
questions.explanation: The Penobscot Nation governs from Indian Island (Panawamskek), a river island that has been a Penobscot center for centuries. The nation retains the islands of the Penobscot River above Old Town under its settlement framework.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Penobscot government sits on Indian Island.

questions.question: The Passamaquoddy Tribe has two reservations in far eastern Maine. They are:
questions.correctAnswer: Sipayik (Pleasant Point) and Motahkomikuk (Indian Township)
distractors: Bar Harbor and Eastport's city lots
questions.explanation: Sipayik, on Passamaquoddy Bay near Eastport, and Motahkomikuk, inland near Princeton, are the Passamaquoddy Tribe's two communities, each with its own local leadership under the tribe's government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two Passamaquoddy homelands: Sipayik and Motahkomikuk.

questions.question: The Mi'kmaq Nation in Maine, federally recognized in 1991, is centered in which part of the state?
questions.correctAnswer: Aroostook County, in northern Maine around Presque Isle
questions.explanation: The Mi'kmaq Nation (formerly the Aroostook Band of Micmacs) is headquartered in Presque Isle. Its people are part of the wider Mi'kmaq nation whose homeland spans the Canadian Maritimes and northern Maine.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Maine's Mi'kmaq are centered in Aroostook.

questions.question: The Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians' homeland follows which river valley in northern Maine?
questions.correctAnswer: The St. John River valley (the Wolastoq)
questions.explanation: The Maliseet - Wolastoqiyik, 'People of the Beautiful River' - are a river people of the St. John (Wolastoq) watershed. The Houlton Band's trust lands are in the Houlton area of Aroostook County.

questions.question: Tribal sovereignty means that a federally recognized tribal nation like the Penobscot Nation:
questions.correctAnswer: Is a self-governing political community whose authority predates the United States and is recognized - not granted - by the federal government
distractors: Is a private cultural association chartered by the state
Has only ceremonial status with no government powers
Is a department of the Maine state government
questions.explanation: Under federal Indian law, tribes are 'domestic dependent nations' whose inherent sovereignty was never surrendered wholesale. Each Maine nation has its own elected government, laws, and courts or justice systems.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sovereignty is inherent, not granted.

img.scene: A tribal council meeting room with a circle of chairs and a carved staff resting on the table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Sovereignty is inherent, not granted.
img.title: INHERENT SOVEREIGNTY

questions.question: Before European colonization, the Wabanaki nations governed themselves and managed their homelands through systems that included:
questions.correctAnswer: Sachems and councils leading by consensus, seasonal rounds of fishing, hunting, planting and gathering, and kinship-based responsibilities to the land
distractors: Hereditary kings ruling from stone capitals
questions.explanation: Wabanaki governance rested on respected leaders, council deliberation, and consensus, fitted to a seasonal economy along rivers and the coast - systems European observers often failed to recognize as government at all.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Consensus, kinship, seasonal rounds.

img.tip: T-Rexy says: Consensus, kinship, seasonal rounds.

questions.question: In the 1700s, the Wabanaki nations dealt with French and British colonial powers through treaties. Those treaties, in Wabanaki understanding and in the written record:
questions.correctAnswer: Established peace, friendship, and trade relations - the Wabanaki did not understand themselves to be surrendering their homelands or their self-government
distractors: Sold all Wabanaki land for trade goods
Made the Wabanaki subjects of the British king in all matters
questions.explanation: A series of treaties from 1725 onward set terms of peace and trade between the Wabanaki and the British Crown. Land loss came mainly through settler encroachment and later state actions, not a single treaty sale.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Treaties meant peace and trade, not surrender.

img.tip: T-Rexy says: Treaties meant peace and trade, not surrender.
img.title: TREATIES OF PEACE AND TRADE

questions.question: After the United States won independence, responsibility for Penobscot and Passamaquoddy treaty obligations in the District of Maine passed to Massachusetts, and then to Maine at statehood. A problem with the land transactions that followed is that:
questions.correctAnswer: Maine and Massachusetts took and sold tribal lands without the federal approvals the U.S. Nonintercourse Act required, which made the transfers legally vulnerable
distractors: The tribes signed away all lands in a single 1820 document
The federal government bought the lands at full price in 1900
No tribal land was ever taken
questions.explanation: The federal Trade and Intercourse Acts barred land purchases from tribes without federal consent. Maine's land dealings lacked that consent - the legal foundation of the land claims case of the 1970s.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Land taken without federal consent could be challenged.

img.scene: Surveyors' chains and old deed papers on a table, the writing blurred and unreadable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Land taken without federal consent could be challenged.
img.title: THE LAND CLAIMS FOUNDATION

questions.question: In the 1970s, the Passamaquoddy and Penobscot sued, claiming a vast portion of Maine as unlawfully taken. The case was resolved by:
questions.correctAnswer: The Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act of 1980 - a federal act, matched by a Maine implementing act, that funded land purchases and a trust in exchange for extinguishing the claims
distractors: A Supreme Court ruling awarding the tribes half of Maine
The tribes withdrawing the claim with nothing
Maine seceding from the settlement process entirely
questions.explanation: The 1980 settlement provided an $81.5 million federal settlement fund - a land-acquisition fund and a trust fund - and the tribes have since bought back hundreds of thousands of acres. It also set the distinctive state-law framework that still shapes tribal-state relations in Maine.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The 1980 Act settled the claims with funds and land.

img.scene: A map table with forested land parcels marked by colored ribbons, no readable labels. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The 1980 Act settled the claims with funds and land.
img.title: THE 1980 SETTLEMENT

questions.question: One way Maine's 1980 settlement differs from the position of most federally recognized tribes in other states is that:
questions.correctAnswer: Maine law treats the tribes in many areas much like municipalities subject to state law, rather than under the usual federal framework of tribal sovereignty - a difference tribal leaders have long sought to change
distractors: Maine tribes may ignore all federal law
Maine tribes are not federally recognized
The settlement gave Maine tribes more sovereignty than any other tribes
questions.explanation: Under the Maine Implementing Act, state law applies broadly on tribal lands, and later federal laws generally do not apply in Maine unless they specifically say so. Restoring the standard federal framework has been the Wabanaki nations' central policy goal in recent decades.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Maine's frame is state law, unlike most states.

img.scene: Two flags flying at different heights outside a government building at dawn. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Maine's frame is state law, unlike most states.
img.title: A DIFFERENT FRAMEWORK

questions.question: Wabanaki studies became a required part of Maine education in 2001, when Maine became the first state to:
questions.correctAnswer: Require by law that Native American history and culture - specifically Wabanaki studies - be taught in its schools
distractors: Require every student to speak a Wabanaki language
Give tribes control of all public schools
questions.explanation: LD 291 (PL 2001, c. 403) required Wabanaki studies as a component of Maine studies under 20-A M.R.S. sec. 4706 - covering tribal governments, cultures, territories, and economic systems. The law was renamed and strengthened as 'Wabanaki studies' in 2023.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Maine required Wabanaki studies first, in 2001.

img.tip: T-Rexy says: Maine required Wabanaki studies first, in 2001.

questions.question: Contemporary Wabanaki governments provide their citizens with services that parallel those of other governments, such as:
questions.correctAnswer: Tribal courts and police, health clinics, housing programs, and natural-resource management including fisheries
questions.explanation: Each Maine tribal nation runs real governments today: courts, law enforcement, health care through tribal clinics, housing, education programs, and stewardship of lands and waters, including sustenance fishing rights.

questions.question: Tribal economic systems in Maine today blend traditional practices with modern enterprises. A signature example is:
questions.correctAnswer: The Passamaquoddy Tribe's management of wild-blueberry lands and other tribal enterprises alongside sustenance fishing, hunting, and gathering rights
distractors: A tribal monopoly on all Maine logging
Tribal ownership of the state's shipyards
questions.explanation: Wabanaki economies combine wage employment, tribal enterprises such as blueberry production and maple operations, and constitutionally and treaty-rooted sustenance practices on tribal lands and waters - economic systems that Maine's Wabanaki studies law names as a required topic.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Old practices and new enterprises together.
